::: {.flashcard-page}

`Result` is how Rust lets a function return either a useful value or a useful
error. The part I had to get comfortable with was that receiving a `Result`
means I still have a decision to make.

::: {.flashcard-stage}
::: {.flashcard-card}

<div class="flashcard-eyebrow">The question</div>

::: {#flashcard-question .flashcard-question role="heading" aria-level="2"}
What should I do with a `Result<T, E>`?
:::

<p class="flashcard-hint">The value can contain success or failure. The caller decides what happens next.</p>

<details class="flashcard-reveal">
  <summary>Reveal the answer</summary>
<div class="flashcard-answer"><p>Match <code>Ok</code> and <code>Err</code>, propagate the error with <code>?</code>, or use <code>unwrap</code> only when a panic is acceptable.</p></div>
</details>
:::
:::

## What a Result contains

The type has two variants:

```rust
enum Result<T, E> {
    Ok(T),
    Err(E),
}
```

`Ok(T)` carries the success value. `Err(E)` carries the error value. Both
types are generic, so a function chooses what success and failure mean for its
own job.

Here is a deliberately small example:

```rust
fn is_even(number: u32) -> Result<String, String> {
    if number % 2 == 0 {
        Ok(format!("{number} is even!"))
    } else {
        Err(format!("{number} is not even!"))
    }
}
```

For this function, both variants contain a `String`. The variant itself tells
me whether the operation succeeded.

## Why unwrap can panic

This is the shortest way to get the success value:

```rust
fn main() {
    let message = is_even(2).unwrap();
    println!("{message}");
}
```

```text
2 is even!
```

But `unwrap` does not handle the error case. It panics if the value is `Err`:

```rust
fn main() {
    let message = is_even(1).unwrap();
    println!("{message}");
}
```

```text
thread 'main' panicked at 'called `Result::unwrap()` on an `Err` value:
"1 is not even!"'
```

::: {.flashcard-block .flashcard-block--gotcha}
<p class="flashcard-block-label">The tradeoff with unwrap</p>

`unwrap` is convenient when a failure really should stop the program, or while
I am writing a quick experiment. It is a poor substitute for deciding how a
real error should be handled.
:::

## Propagate the error with question mark

The `?` operator extracts the value from `Ok`. If it sees `Err`, it returns that
error from the current function:

```rust
fn print_even(number: u32) -> Result<(), String> {
    let message = is_even(number)?;
    println!("{message}");
    Ok(())
}

fn main() -> Result<(), String> {
    print_even(2)?;
    Ok(())
}
```

The function using `?` must return a compatible error type. Here both
`print_even` and `main` return `Result<_, String>`, so the error can move up the
call stack unchanged.

## Handle both variants with match

When I want different behavior for success and failure, `match` makes both
paths explicit:

```rust
fn main() {
    match is_even(1) {
        Ok(message) => println!("{message}"),
        Err(error) => println!("Could not continue: {error}"),
    }
}
```

```text
Could not continue: 1 is not even!
```

No panic, and no error path hidden from the reader. This is more typing than
`unwrap`, but it gives me full control.

::: {.flashcard-block .flashcard-block--remember}
<p class="flashcard-block-label">What I keep in my head</p>

Use `match` when both paths need behavior, `?` when the caller should handle the
error, and `unwrap` only when stopping immediately is the intended behavior.
:::
